content: Central venous catheters (CVCs) are essential tools in managing both acute and chronic illnesses. The dressings and securement devices used for CVCs must prevent the catheter from becoming dislodged, protect against microbial colonization and infection, and ensure patient comfort. A wide variety of dressing and securement products are available for clinical use. The objective of this review was to compare different dressing and securement devices for CVCs in terms of their impact on catheter-related bloodstream infections (BSIs), catheter colonization, entryand exit-site infections, skin colonization, skin irritation, catheter securement failure, dressing condition, and mortality. A comprehensive search was conducted in June 2015 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, DARE, NHSEED, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, EBSCO CINAHL, and six clinical trial registries. There were no restrictions on language, publication date, or study setting. Randomized controlled trials evaluating the effects of dressing and securement devices for all types of CVCs were included, such as shortand long-term CVCs, tunnelled and non-tunnelled catheters, port-a-caths, haemodialysis catheters, and peripherally-inserted central catheters (PICCs). Standard Cochrane Collaboration methods were used for data collection and analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the relevance of studies, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for categorical data, and rate ratios with standard errors for outcomes measured over time. A multiple treatment meta-analysis was performed to rank the effectiveness of each intervention for each outcome. The review included 22 studies involving 7,436 participants, comparing nine different types of securement devices or dressings. Most studies had an unclear or high risk of performance bias due to the visible differences in the dressings and securement devices. The extent of blinding in outcome assessment was unclear in many studies. The quality of evidence varied across comparisons and outcomes, with frequent downgrades for imprecision, indirectness, risk of bias, and inconsistency. The evidence did not clearly demonstrate a difference in the rate of catheter-related BSIs between securement with gauze and tape versus standard polyurethane (SPU) dressings (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.63, low-quality evidence). Similarly, the comparison between chlorhexidine gluconate-impregnated (CGI) dressings and SPU dressings showed no clear difference in catheter-related BSI rates (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.40 to 1.05, moderate-quality evidence). However, there is high-quality evidence that medication-impregnated dressings reduce the incidence of catheter-related BSIs compared to all other dressing types (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.93). Moderate-quality evidence suggests that CGI dressings reduce the frequency of catheter-related BSIs per 1,000 patient days compared to SPU dressings (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.78). CGI dressings also appear to reduce catheter tip colonization compared to SPU dressings (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.73, moderate-quality evidence). However, the relative effects of gauze and tape versus SPU dressings on catheter tip colonization remain unclear (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.77, very low-quality evidence). The evidence is inconclusive regarding differences in rates of skin irritation or damage when comparing CGI dressings to SPU dressings (RR 11.17, 95% CI 0.84 to 149.48, moderate-quality evidence). A multiple treatment meta-analysis suggested that sutureless securement devices are likely the most effective at reducing catheter-related BSIs, with CGI dressings ranked second. However, this conclusion is based on low-quality evidence. In conclusion, medication-impregnated dressings appear to reduce the incidence of catheter-related BSIs compared to other dressing types. CGI dressings may also reduce catheter-related BSIs, catheter tip colonization, and infection frequency per 1,000 patient days compared to SPU dressings. Sutureless securement devices may be the most effective at reducing catheter-related BSIs, but the evidence supporting this is of low quality. Most studies included in this review were conducted in intensive care unit (ICU) settings. Further high-quality research is needed to better understand the relative effectiveness of dressing and securement products for CVCs and to evaluate new products.
